text_fidelity_a: Jabra SUPREME Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging - Black I had always found the Motorola H700 flip headset to be the best and most convenient bluetooth solution. Its performance was good and  the flip microphone made it easy to carry in a holster. Unfortunately it finally died and they are out of production. So I decided to try this headset and was pleasantly surprised. This actually surpasses the Motorola H700. Voice recognition by my iPhone is improved - presumably because of the better noise reduction of the headset, the calls seem very clear on both ends, and the talking caller ID is a real plus.It can fit in the same holster I used for my H700 - though it is a bit large for it. If I can find a holster with a belt clip, this could be a real winner. The only con is that it isn't extremely comfortable on the earlobe after a few hours. The bar that holds the ear clip to the unit is a bit too long I think and the end poking through tends to be a little irritating. It comes with an additional ear pad and clip but there is not really any more comfort using either of those. I have not tried the "comfort kit" - sold separately for way too much money. When I first saw the "comfort kit" advertised I was amused that a $100 bluetooth headset would need an additional expenditure  to be comfortable. However I may be forced to try it if I can't get  the ear clip adjusted properly. Jabra should be embarrassed by this.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra SUPREME Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging - Black

Firstly, the ear loops are awkward and tend to shift and drop a lot while wearing, so the ear buds often come unseated from your outer ear canal. The over-ear clips are heavy and awkward, so they significantly bend and pull your ears down and you end up looking like Dumbo (at least I do lol).

The bigger issue, for me, is that there is a real problem in audio quality. No matter what I listen to, there is cracking and splitting in the audio. At first, I thought the splitting might be from a bad bluetooth connection, so I tried pairing these with several devices, but it remained. And the cracking occurs in tandem with percussion, which leads me to believe the issues have more to do with the audio quality than a connection issue.

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA 360W Surge Protector Battery Power Backup - 8 Outlets, Black I'm pleased with the performance and features of this UPS. While it does not have the features that my other UPS's have (such as a screen that displays battery status, load, etc.) that's a plus, since I don't often use, or need, the info on the screen. This has just a simple on/off button, a mute button, and basic LED indicators that show if it's on line power or battery power.

It comes with the battery leads detached. Before use you need to remove the battery access panel (very simple -- just two screws) and connect the battery (also a very simple process).

I use it to for my router and cable modem so I can maintain Internet access and wifi during a power outage. I've simulated a power outage and both the modem and router didn't skip a beat. While this has a smaller capacity than the UPS's I use for my PCs, the 1000VA 550W specs are more than adequate to maintain a long run time given the light load.

One quibble -- and I have the same one with most UPS systems -- is that the outlets are too closely spaced, making it difficult to use all of them when plugging in devices that have a wall wart at the end. I would also have liked to see the outlets be color coded so you can more easily tell the difference between the bank of outlets that are surge protected only, and the bank that is surge/battery protected.

Those quibbles aside, it's been a good performer that provides all the features needed at a decent price.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA 360W Surge Protector Battery Power Backup - 8 Outlets, Black

I saw that this one was cheap and had mostly positive reviews, so I thought I'd take a chance on it. With free super saver shipping, it arrived in about a week and a half and it was exactly as I expected it would be from reading the reviews. It is true what several of the reviews have mentioned, the screws that come with it truly do not hold the end cap in the case (which means that the hard drive can slip in and out). It was a fairly simple fix; I just had to find some other screws that actually held it together. Another thing that's been mentioned is that there is no way to turn the enclosure off, i.e. if the drive is plugged into the computer it will be on regardless of if the computer is on or not (at least in my experience).

Conclusion: A good product if you need/want a hard drive enclosure and don't want to spend a lot. Having to find different screws and not being able to turn the drive off without unplugging it from the computer keep it from being five stars.

That's my two cents.

Sony WF-1000XM4 Industry Leading Noise Canceling Truly Wireless Earbud Headphones with Alexa Built-in, Black This is my first purchase of earbuds in the over $200 category. I got the Jabra Elite 65t as soon as they came out and have since bought a couple of other pairs of earbuds in the under $100 category that had better features like IPX7 or 8hr battery life. Therefore I was excited to upgrade to the XM4 for their bettery life and the noise canceling.

Unfortunately, I've had several issues with these. I don't have particularly small ears. Usually the medium tips fit without issue. On the XM4, I started with the medium tips and tested their air tightness using the app. The small tips don't have any kind of seal on my ears without really shoving them super far down my ear canal, so I decided to stick with the medium size. Unfortunately, I have experienced significant ear fatigue enough so that I can't wear the earbuds for more than a couple of hours. I have since switched to the small tips for the sake of comfort, but that means sacrificing any passive noise canceling - and unless I have a defective unit, without the passive noise canceling in addition to the active noise canceling, there is absolutely no difference between having the noise canceling on and off. To me, this completely defeats the purpose of buying noise canceling earbuds.

I also have had issues with connectivity such as the bluetooth connection on my phone suddenly dropping and having to go into the app to manually pair them again.

In terms of battery life, depending on the control settings of each earbud, there can be a difference in the drain of battery between the left and right side. On a bad day, I had a 30% difference with the right draining significantly faster. My earbuds are using the factory settings with the playback controls on the right and the noise canceling on the left for reference.

Both the connectivity problems and the bettery difference between the earbuds has seemed to have gotten better since performing a factory reset, but be aware that there is still a little difference in the rate of battery drain between the L and R earbuds (It's not super significant now and maybe reaches under 7-8% difference at the end of the day).

I bought some Comply foam tips, which I hope will fix the discomfort issue and make the noise canceling work at the optimal rate without the ear fatigue. However, I shouldn't have to modify almost $300 earbuds to make them work like they should. It would help if Sony would offer more sizes of ear tips to help make them more usable for a wider population. Then again, if I have gripes like these, then maybe the XM4s aren't for me. Makes me super sad considering I think that they're probably fantastic for most people.
text_fidelity_b: Sony WF-1000XM4 Industry Leading Noise Canceling Truly Wireless Earbud Headphones with Alexa Built-in, Black

text_fidelity_a:
eufy security, SoloCam E40, Outdoor Security Camera, Advanced AI Person-Detection, Two-Way Audio, 2K Resolution, 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi Only, IP65 Weatherproof, No Monthly Fee I contacted Eufy after the battery died after 4 weeks. Took them 2 days to send me an autobot emailed response to which I responded that I wanted a live person to email me. Another 2 days, and a person asked me to send a screen shot of the battery settings. REALLY??? So I did that which my battery settings were for optimized battery life. Another 2 days and still no answer. There was an option on the bottom of their email to escalate the case to management if I was not happy with the response, and that they would get back to me within 24 hours. So I clicked it, and explained how I was not getting a response. But guess what? I never got a response. So five days later, I decided to return this because I'm still in the return window. Maybe I had a defective unit. We have had a very mild winter, so I cannot imagine that the weather would make a supposed four-month battery charge only last for four weeks. Plus, there isn't much motion going on to drain the battery either. Sometimes, 3 or 4 days go by with no motion. The most number of times it has detected motion in one day is four times. So it's not like the battery is getting drained from the camera being triggered 10 times a day. I'm going to try one more time, and watch the battery life to see how quickly it drains before the return window closes.

**** Update **** The replacement camera will have a battery life of approximately 6 or 7 weeks, judging by the amount of battery used thus far. Since the return window is just 4 weeks, I have returned this camera again and will not try another one. 6-7 weeks battery life is better than 4 weeks, for sure. But still disappointing because Eufy advertises a 4 month battery life. I would have been willing to try to Eufy 2 Pro that has a 365-day battery life (figuring it probably really only has a 6 month battery life). But this would mean purchasing a home base. Also, the location of the camera does not get any direct sunlight, so even a solar panel would not have helped. If you are looking for just one camera that is wireless, and you aren't interested in having to take it down every month or two for recharging, this is not the camera for you. Their customer support contacted me the day after I wrote my first review. (I couldn't get any support previously through their normal channels.)
text_fidelity_b: eufy security, SoloCam E40, Outdoor Security Camera, Advanced AI Person-Detection, Two-Way Audio, 2K Resolution, 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi Only, IP65 Weatherproof, No Monthly Fee

text_fidelity_a:
Legrand - Wiremold Cable Management Kit, Cord Organizer and Hider, Concealer, C210S Cord Cover Kit, White I'm sure they do it for shipping purposes and to appeal to homeowners without tools, but I don't like that they give you multiple short pieces instead of fewer long pieces that you could cut down to appropriate size. That just means you need more couplers; each additional coupler decreases the appeal of the final installation.

Honestly, I hate surface mounted conduit. But there are times when it is required, and in those cases better than nothing. I own my home, so of course I put all permanent links properly inside the walls, but even then, there are times when the Cat/RG/other jacks are not directly behind the furniture holding the devices that need the cables. In these cases, I prefer to mount these with screws, and then caulk and paint them into the painted baseboards so they blend in better, although they have made these with tape for truly temporary installations.

There is just one connector for an inside corner and an outside corner (on the x/z axis). And in my opinion, these are the only two you should really need, and you probably need more of them. I am never going vertical up walls with cables; I just go from the jack along the baseboard to behind the furniture...if I need more than that, I'm afraid I need to just stop being lazy and tear down a wall or something.

I get that if you are in an apartment or a rental property, you may need more flexibility with this. But in my opinion, if you can't do a proper wall-mount TV install without surface-mount conduit, then you should just use a TV stand as God intended because this is not enough to make cables acceptable in such an install (although honestly, it is better than nothing).
text_fidelity_b: Legrand - Wiremold Cable Management Kit, Cord Organizer and Hider, Concealer, C210S Cord Cover Kit, White

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR Nighthawk 4-Stream AX4 Wi-fi 6 Router (RAX40) – AX3000 Wireless Speed (Up to 3 Gbps) | 1,500 Sq Ft Coverage Bought this router a few days ago and have already begun the return process. I didn't have a good gut feeling about this router from the start, partly because the reviews are not all raves and partly simply because it looks kind of...evil to me. I am definitely not a fan of the hyper-aggressive router design trend that seems to be targeted at adolescent male gamers. I do not look at this thing and think it looks cool and feel positive feelings; I look at it and feel...apprehension. As a physical object, it's not something I really want in my apartment. But I decided to give it a try anyway because I don't think that kind of gut feeling should be one's primary consideration in choosing a router, and because I often like having the latest, cutting-edge tech and thought it would be nice to be ready for Wifi 6 for when I eventually get an iPhone 11 or some other device that features that protocol. But unfortunately, the negative experiences do not come only when I look at the thing.

I was at first alarmed, as I set up the router, by what a very long time it took anything to happen in the app. At every point at which I so much as switched to a different screen in the app, both during and after setup, the app would chug for an alarmingly long time before finally displaying the page I'd navigated to. This is to be expected when the router needs to restart, but...these were not points at which the router needed to restart. These were not points at which I'd changed any setting at all. These were points at which nothing at all had happened except that I'd attempted to go from, say, the app's main page to the Device Manager page, or the Wifi Settings page, or wherever. Simply switching pages in the app would take 20 or 30 seconds or longer. Another negative first impression.

I also noticed that the app doesn't give me access to a lot of the features of the router I expect to have access to. Granted, I'm an advanced user compared to a lot of people - networking is an aspect of computing I've enjoyed mucking around in for decades now, and my inclination with a new router (or an old one, for that matter) is to dive straight into areas of the settings where many ordinary users may fear to tread. But the Nighthawk phone app appears to be targeted more toward the average consumer. Which, if you're more the average consumer, is fine. But if you're me, you find that to be a disappointing restriction.

Then I started trying to use the web UI instead, and while it gave me access to all those more techy parameters I sought, I found the same delay problem happening when I tried to switch from one page of settings to another, but here it happened for longer, and sometimes the target page wouldn't load at all until I clicked again, this time on the blank page with the spinning progress indicator in the center.

So both of the means I have for interfacing with the router are inordinately slow, and one of them is clunky and glitchy on top of it.

And finally, add to all this the way I will occasionally go to navigate to any ordinary webpage and be told my browser can't display the page because I'M NOT CONNECTED TO THE INTERNET, and voila! - the straw that broke the proverbial camel's back.

This happens, and I go and look at the router to see if maybe it's restarted itself for some reason (automatic software update?) and...no. All lights are on and looking as they do during normal operation; the router's just not providing said normal operation.

I never once had such problems with the Apple AirPort Extreme I replaced with this router, nor with the Linksys AC5400 I bought more recently and then wound up giving to a friend. So, because I want a router that, unlike the AirPort Extreme, is tri-band, is still supported with software/firmware updates, and might also feature better performance with multiple connected devices, I bought myself another AC5400 with which I will be replacing this unsatisfactory Netgear thing as soon as it arrives.

And also because I decided I can wait for Wifi 6 until such time as I actually do have devices capable of taking advantage of it, which may be quite some time (i just bought a new MacBook Pro which doesn't support it, and I don't see the iPhone 11 as having any compelling advantages over my iPhone XS Max, soooo...).

The Linksys AC5400 is a monster among 802.11ac routers and has garnered much respect in tech mags and blogs and so forth. Plus I myself have about a year's experience with one and it's been fast, reliable, and glitch-free. So if you're looking for a new router and don't feel compelled to buy into 802.11ax just yet (few devices support it yet anyways), I heartily recommend that one.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Nighthawk 4-Stream AX4 Wi-fi 6 Router (RAX40) – AX3000 Wireless Speed (Up to 3 Gbps) | 1,500 Sq Ft Coverage

text_fidelity_a:
SABRENT Rocket Q 500GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive R/W 2000/1000MB/s (SB-RKTQ-500) Compared to the Crucial 1TB M2 NVME I reviewed earlier, this Sabrent 512GB model benchmarks a little faster. And it works just fine on a PCI M2 adapter card, which are only a few bucks. (I bought the cheapest one available and it works.)

The NVME still offers much faster R/W speeds than other drives even when used with SATA 1 (as on my workstation). For example, the SSD I was using as my hard disk benchmarks at about 220MB/second. The Sabrent NVME on a PCI card benchmarks at about 1.5GB/second.

This time I experimented to see if I could get Debian Linux distro running on the NVME on my older workstation.

It took a few tries. Getting the OS to boot directly from the NVME was a no-go. Since the NVME is mounted on an adapter card, I had hoped it would trick the system into thinking it was just an ordinary SATA drive and boot from it. But that didn't happen.

So what I did was installed all the Linux OS EXCEPT for the boot folder on the NVME, and put the boot folder on the SSD HDD. So it boots from the SSD but the entire OS is on the NVME and runs from it.

Step one:

The partition manager in the Debian installer didn't want to partition the NVME at first.

So I bailed out of it and used GParted (Gnome disks utility couldn't do this) to "create partition table" and selected msdos as type. That wiped everything and turned the whole drive into unallocated space. From that point the partition manager worked.

Step two:

From the linux bootable USB installer I partitioned the SSD (not the NVME) with a primary partition labeled (to be mounted) as /boot. (You can make this partition most any size from a few GB on up---the boot files don't require a lot of space.) The remaining space I manually labeled as /msc.

I partitioned the NVME so the installer would put everything else on it, starting with / (root). You can simply make the whole NVME / root and the installer will take care of putting everything else on that drive, or you can do what I did and set up size-defined partitions for /home, /usr, and so on.

After installing the system, the installer asks where you want the bootloader GRUB installed. I selected the SSD.

It worked. The SSD does the booting to the NVME, which then runs the OS. And it did improve speed.
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT Rocket Q 500GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive R/W 2000/1000MB/s (SB-RKTQ-500)

text_fidelity_a:
Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10 You may know about the announcement from Lenovo a few weeks ago that going forward the company will be certifying all their ThinkPad and Thinkstation workstations for Linux. This computer is an IdeaCentre, not a ThinkPad or ThinkStation, and it comes preloaded with Windows, but I am a Linux user and I wanted to see if it will run Linux.

First things first: If you're looking for a gaming computer or something to handle graphics-intensive programs, this isn't it. It doesn't have a screaming fast processor, although it is a capable one. The onboard AMD Raven graphics module is pretty capable (I tried it out on a big display), but this model has no expansion slot for a video or audio card or any other such upgrades.

It does have a bay for a big 3.5 inch HDD with SATA connectors. And it comes with a 256GB SSD already installed on the motherboard. It also comes with 4GB RAM (and a second slot to add more), and a wired keyboard and mouse and the power supply. It has four USB 2.0 ports in the back, and two 2.0 and two 3.0 (gen 1) USB ports in the front. Also on the front are a card reader slot, the optical drive, mic and headset connection ports, and the power button. The back also has an HDMI port, VGA-out port, and and ethernet port.

It's about the size of an ITX mini tower form factor box, which is a little larger than a big dictionary. It stands upright, so the footprint is pretty small. And it's lightweight compared to a big desktop box.

I didn't even complete the first boot into Windows before attempting a Linux install. Tapping F2 on boot will get you into a graphical menu for picking your boot device, and F12 will get you into a deeper menu for selecting boot order and into the BIOS.

My favorite distro is Debian, so I thought I'd take a shot at installing it. It was a no-go. It didn't have the drivers for the onboard Atheros wifi card, and apparently a few other things. I actually pulled the wifi card off the motherboard and substituted a dongle and gave it a second try. I got Debian installed, but the machine still froze on boot without ever getting into the desktop environment.

So I tried installing Ubuntu, which, along with Red Hat, was specifically mentioned as now being supported by Lenovo. Success. Installation went smoothly. I was still using the dongle for wifi, so I shut down the machine and reinstalled the inboard card. Again, success. Wifi operated right away.

The couple of minor -- emphasizing minor -- things I don't like is that an inboard white LED glows continually when the power supply is plugged in, and as far as I can tell there's no way to turn it off.

Bottom line here is I think it's a good machine for general use. It's pretty capable, but be aware of its limitations so you won't be disappointed.
text_fidelity_b: Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White I've had my two Echo Dots for one year now. Now, a year later, Google Home has really come forward by leaps and bounds while Alexa has basically stayed exactly the same. For Android users, the easiest way to describe it is that the Alexa has become an iPhone vs. Google's Android. I think I am the norm in that there is almost no "Skill" I have use for with Alexa. Instead I ask things that are already built in features: weather, time, set alarm, add things to shopping list, and of course, control home devices like lights. However, ALL home devices can do those things just as easily and intuitively as Alexa does, so to see if you are getting the best device you need to compare other features:

Asking a question - Google wins hands down. Google uses... Google, to get your answer. Alexa uses Bing I think, nuff said. Most of the time the response from my Dot is "I'm sorry, I don't know that" and if it does "know", it is giving an answer to something I'm not truly asking. For example, I asked it what movies were playing on FOX tonight and the response was "I'm still learning about fox. Ask me a fox fact so I can learn more about them." Many times it even just answers to search the internet. Well, if I have to search the internet then I want to use Google to do it and there is no way to set your search engine. Essentially every time it tells me to search the internet, what I hear in my mind is "Use Google" - yeah, I think I just might, Amazon.

"Skills" apps - all but useless for every day life. Skills I can see some possibility of using are the reading a bedtime story if you have kids, or asking Alexa to play a game. But for adult life and for truly being a life/home assistant to you, none of the Skills compare at all to the platform that Google already has in place from decades of being an internet powerhouse. Example: finding your phone. This is a pretty common issue that I think it's reasonable to assume any of these home assist devices should be able to tackle easily. For Alexa you must download a "Skill" (there are a few to choose from) and register your phone number to that app. The major flaws with Alexa doing this are: 1. you need to first tell Alexa to open and use the skill with precise wording for it to work (i.e. "Alexa find my phone" won't work. "Alexa have Tracker find my phone" won't work. "Alexa open the Tracker app. Alexa have Tracker find my phone" won't work. "Alexa open the Tracker app. Alexa ask the Tracker app to find my phone" works). 2. if your ringer is off there is no ability to turn it on for the purpose of finding the phone. Essentially you'd be better off to add "me" to contacts with your own number and just tell Alexa "call me" because that is all you are getting with Alexa's "Skills", it's easier to just do that, and it only has the same flaw of not ringing if ringer is off. In comparison, with Google you download nothing, simply say "Google find my phone", and viola, your phone will ring whether the ringer is on or not. Google also has "Maps" which is huge. "Maps" gives you locations, hours of operation, can list like-businesses, tell you how to get somewhere and how long it will take you, and even tell you which buses to take if you have public transit in your area, etc. Alexa can only utilize Yelp and if a business isn't on Yelp then Alexa has no access to even the very basic info Yelp supplies (hours).

There's one 'Pro' to Echo over any other home device, and that is as it relates to other Amazon devices. Like Google, Amazon is also an internet powerhouse in it's own way. Having a Prime membership is the norm rather than the exception in most households, and obviously that means asking Echo to order something or play a Prime movie or Prime music is going to be smooth and easy with the Echo. Also, where Amazon still leads the pack is with it's Fire Stick, and again, obviously, Echo is going to be well integrated with that device, while other Home Assistants aren't given that level of access to integrate as well. So that's why I give it 2 stars - because I can't use my FireStick AS EASILY if I owned something other than an Echo. But I can still use the remote so that ability is def not worth more than two stars, especially when Google has the ability to take away access to things like YouTube (which it did) from Amazon in retaliation for being denied access to things like FireStick integration into it's own device.

Bottom line, Echo/Alexa seems great until you see how much better the later competitors to the market have improved on the user experience and are continuing to improve by leaps and bounds with each new update, while Amazon rests on 'we were the first'. Or, in other words, don't fall for yet another same ol' iPhone that is introducing features Android users have had for at least five years when instead you could just buy the Android and have the newest and best features right now.
text_fidelity_b: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White

text_fidelity_a:
Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red) I really hate to use the word “cute” but there’s no way around it – this is a cute cam! It looks pretty much the same as the original Cube, but offers improved video and the addition of WiFi. Of the new features, the WiFi is the most significant, and makes this far more useful as a cam.

I also have the original Cube and the build quality continues to be very good. These are priced higher than the “no name” action cams, but after using (and breaking) a couple of those, it’s nice to be able to count on the Cube to keep on working. It’s water resistant, which makes it less worrisome when using it in bad weather or around water. It supports up to a 128MB SD card

The form factor and overall design is much the same as the original Cube. It has a magnet in the base that is more than strong enough to keep it well-planted. It’s not strong enough for significant activity (e.g., staying on a bike handle while riding) but it offers the benefit of tripod-like stability without the need for a tripod (providing you have something metal to fasten the magnet).

The biggest change is wifi on the Cube+. I found the setup to be straightforward – basically just download the app and follow the setup steps. I love that the app lets you use it as a live view – that’s a big improvement over the original Cube. It’s a very helpful feature for planning a shot, plus allows me to monitor how things are turning out without having to play the video.

Image quality has been impressive – zero complaints there. I was pleased with the resolution of the original Cube, and this is a bit better. Audio quality is OK. It’s not outstanding, but it clearly picks up voices. I understand that earlier versions of the Cube+ had very poor sound quality, but the one I have (got it in Dec 2015) is fine with regard to sound.

All in all, it’s a great cam with a fun form factor and look. Well worth considering if you’re looking for a small profile action cam with solid build quality and performance. While the price has increased over that of the original Cube, the wifi features are very useful and well implemented, making this version well worth the additional cost.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red)

Of course I have other Wi-Fi devices. That should NOT be a problem.

This is NOT ready for prime time … no pun intended.

I do NOT intend to have to set up this device every couple hours.

The second connection attempt failed. Nothing wrong with my Wi-Fi or my internet connection. Maybe the problem is that it is raining.

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation This is a great streaming box! Like the title says, it's a ROKU on steroids. I have an Apple Airport Extreme router and the ROKU would "occasionally" start buffering because of the processor; however, with the Amazon Fire TV, that's not an issue because it has a quad-core processor. Great streaming box!

Updated 5-4-14 I've had the Fire TV for a couple of months now and for the most part it's great; however, today we rented "Bad Grandpa" on Amazon. It played great but when there was 35 mins left in the movie, it quit playing. Tried to restart the movie and got a message saying there was a problem with playing the movie and to contact Amazon Customer Service. I called them and they said that when this happens, "...unplug the Fire TV for 15 seconds and then plug it back in." In my opinion, that takes the fun out of watching a movie! I thought the memory and quad-core processor would be enough to stop this from happening, wrong! Having said that, instead of naming my review "ROKU on Steroids" I should have named it "Just like ROKU".

The Amazon rep said that it was a problem with the memory of the Amazon Fire TV and not the video. When asked if the problem could be fixed by Amazon with an update, all he said was "I'll forward that to Amazon".

If you don't mind watching videos that stop playing and having to unplug the Fire TV and restart it during a movie, you'll really like the Fire TV.

One other point, the Amazon rep stated that it might be my router. I have an Apple Airport Extreme, the best and fastest available. If it was my router, I guess the Amazon rep should have had me unplug my router instead of the Fire TV. He finally admitted that it was the Fire TV and not the router.

Just wanted to get this information out there so people can be informed about the Amazon Fire TV before purchasing one. All in all, I'm happy with the Fire TV...just aggravated that I have to unplug it and restart it when watching movies. The Amazon Fire TV should be better than this!
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation

text_fidelity_a: APC Surge Protector with Telephone, DSL and Coaxial Protection, P11VT3, 3020 Joules, 11 Outlet Surge Protector Power Strip Gray I have been using APC products professionally for years, as part of my job with FEMA. All of our computers, servers, modems, routers and printers are connected through APC UPS units with built in surge protectors, or units like this one,. FEMA goes into areas where storms happen frequently and with great ferocity. Power interruptions and surges are very common. A few months ago, we had an electrical storm in our area, lots of lighting and thunder. We took a pretty good hit somewhere near our house which knocked out power for a pretty large area, and caused some damage to the grid. Unfortunately, the little power strip that I have all my home network gear plugged into didn't stop the surge and it blew out the internal fax modem of my all-in-one printer. (I'm rather disappointed that the house circuit breakers didn't provide enough protection. This is a new home.) Now, we don't fax every day. But, when you need it, you need it and don't want to go to UPS store to fax a simple one page document. We did this for a while. But, finally, I broke down and got a new printer. So, this time, it's going to be well protected. As is everything else in my home network equipment. This APC unit protects ALL of the connections, phone, ethernet, coax AND electrical. It even comes with jumpers for all three data connections. $25 is a small price to pay, to protect over $2,000 worth of equipment. Oh, and just remember that most surge protectors have to be replaced like every three years. This one comes with a LIFETIME warranty with $1000 equipment replacement guarantee. So, good purchase. Five stars.

Sudio N2 Pro True Wireless Bluetooth in-Ear Earbuds with ANC - Multipoint Connection, IPX4 Water Resistant, USB-C and Wireless Charging, Microphone, 30h Play Time with Charging Case (Blue) I’ve used the Sudio N2 Pro Earbuds for about a month, and I like them. I typically wear them for about 2-3 hours a day while working at my desk, and I have two major pros and three major cons I’ve noticed during the last month.

PROS:
🎵 The earbuds are super comfortable! I have multiple inner ear piercings in both ears (rook, daith, tragus) and a LOT of earbuds hurt after about thirty minutes. I can wear the Sudio N2s for several hours at a time. Small, medium, and large silicone tips are included so you can get a good fit depending on your ears. Sometimes I walk around my house and do chores with these in, they haven’t fallen out once.

🎵 For earbuds, the ANC is good! I can actually notice a difference with the ANC on and off; with some earbuds that claim to have noise cancelling, there’s really no difference. The ANC on the Sudio N2s blocks out when the television is playing in the next room, and even muffles the sound of the heater right under my desk.

CONS:
🎵 Battery life is not great. With ANC on, I get 4 hours, maaaaybe 4.5 if I’m lucky. I put the case on my charging pad every other day, it seems. The case supports wireless charging, which is a positive, or via USB-C. I’ve noticed the earbuds don’t always turn off when put in the case and the lid is closed, which undoubtedly contributes to the faster battery drain.

🎵 The earbuds support Multipoint connection, or connecting to multiple devices, but I can only get them to connect to my Mac. No matter what I try, they will not connect to my phone (Samsung Note 20 Ultra). I tried every suggestion in the online manual, but I can’t even get the earbuds to factory reset.

🎵 The touch controls are VERY sensitive. I have to make sure I don’t have any video tabs open when I put them in, or the video starts blasting in my ear. The only audible cue I noticed was to turn ANC on, and that is “Noise Cancelling.” A beep indicates turning it off, and beeps are used for all other cues. I don’t know what does what, I just wish I could turn them off.

Although the cons slightly outweigh the pros, I still use the Sudio N2s every day. The comfort is a huge factor for me. I’ve tried probably 8 pairs of earbuds in the last year, and this is the only pair I can wear for more than an hour at a time.

Ring Video Doorbell (1st Gen) – 720p HD video, motion activated alerts, easy installation – Satin Nickel The lifetime warranty on this doorbell is the real deal. This is a very well-supported doorbell.

I was having issues with holiday season package thieves and a non-working wireless doorbell. Ring is the only video doorbell I could find that will work wirelessly. The first one had battery issues. Replaced no problem. The second one had sound issues. Replaced no problem. The third on works FLAWLESSLY. I absolutely love it.

The smart motion sensor works well. I see everyone who comes onto my porch, but not my neighbors' porches (three doors lined up on one big house). Two way sound is mostly good -> if it's really windy, it's hard to hear sometimes. The video is way better than I thought it would be. I can see well enough on my phone, but if I download and watch on my computer, it is very impressive.

I signed up for the cloud recording - it's the least expensive pay service of any of my security cameras, and it has been reliable over the few weeks I have been using it. The doorbell is also conspicuous enough to act as a deterrent. I've had a couple of alerts where people looked like they were going to come up the steps and then changed their minds. Both my postal carrier and my UPS driver said that a lot of their stops have these, and they really like them.

Bottom line: It took a couple of tries, but I am one hundred percent happy with this doorbell. If you have an issue, use the warranty. It's a real thing.

UPDATE: I have a CHIME now, as well, and it also works beautifully. The Ring Company gave it to me for free as a promotion, because I had bought two of their doorbells.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell (1st Gen) – 720p HD video, motion activated alerts, easy installation – Satin Nickel

text_fidelity_a:
SABRENT 4TB Rocket NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive (SB-ROCKET-4TB) So, I've had this thing for a few months, and it is no longer working. I put my OS (Win10) on it, and everything seemed fine. The NVMe has a heat shield on it that has a fan, so the temps never got as high as some people have reported.

However, the performance of my computer slowly declined until I could no longer rely on the computer to not crash randomly within 30 minutes of starting it. Everything was failing. I could not figure out what the heck was going on. Started troubleshooting everything. Couldn't get through a memtest, so I bought some new ram so I can use my computer while I wait for the G.Skill RMA process. However, even with the new ram, the PC cannot boot with the Sabrent NVMe. Does not proceed further than the loading screen.

Tried booting into safe mode, which failed, as well as resetting the computer through the windows troubleshooting tool. Nothing would go past the loading screen. I've added another photo showing that substantial loss of performance, even while it is not being used by anything else. Keep in mind that although the numbers are mostly higher than the SATA SSD, a loss in performance like this is a tell-tale sign that it is failing. If you notice something similar with your hardware, back up what you want to keep immediately.

Tried booting from my older SSD, and was able to boot just fine. I am still somehow able to access the information on the NVMe when booting from another SSD, but the system is unstable while running on it. I will continue to try to get a replacement or a refund before conceding that I have a $120 tax for trying to save money.

I tried to use the tool to check if there was a firmware update. Doesn't work, as it said cannot find information on the hardware. This is with the latest everything. Seemed odd, so I sent an email to the bug reporting email they provide. Got a response from google saying that email does not exist....

I reached out to Sabrent technical support. No response after a week.

I'm very disappointed. I've gotten other sabrent hardware before and hadn't had problems. Looks like their memory is not their game. Even worse that their customer support is non-existent. Don't expect to get help if you run into the same issue that I got.

I'd recommend spending the extra $20 or $30 to get hardware that has a record of reliability, like samsung (the much older SSD that still works, and and using right now to be able to even use my computer is the 840 EVO).
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT 4TB Rocket NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive (SB-ROCKET-4TB)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Harmony 900 Rechargeable Remote with Color Touch Screen (Discontinued by Manufacturer) First let me start by saying I am an IT professional and have been a audiophile and video hobbyist for many years. Naturally I have had a lot of different audio / video equipment over the years. I had a computer hooked up to my TV long before it was in fashion. And finally, I am always looking for the next great gadget on the market. Enter the Harmony 900.

Here is my current setup in my living room:
Samsung TV HL-T5687
Sony PS3 Move
Nyko IR Adaptor for PS3 - Media Hub Slim
Roku2 XS
Onkyo TX-NR808
Sharp DVDR-VCR DV-RW340
Cable Box Motorola DVR DCH-3416
Shuttle PC with Media Center
X10 Home Automation - Various Devices

I basically use my TV as a monitor, the only cable plugged into it is the HDMI from the receiver. Hence, the Onkyo receiver does all the sound and switching between inputs.

The Harmony 900 Experience:

I did a lot of research before buying this $250.00 remote. Considering this thing is 50.00 more that my Kindle Fire and does a whole lot less, it wasn't easy pulling the trigger.

Ergonomics:
I read the good and bad reviews and decided that this one would best fit my needs. From many of the negative reviews I concluded the biggest concern was going to be dropping it and breaking the screen. It becomes very obvious why this is the minute you put it in your hand. It is very sleek and conforms well to your hand, but is as a slippery as a fresh water eel in your hand. Also due to the few contact points with any surface other than the charger, it is very easy to slide off a couch arm or get bumped off a coffee table.

That being said, the remote is very well balanced and fits nicely in the hand. The buttons are raised and easy to push. However some of the buttons are simply in the wrong spot. The volume and channel buttons should be reversed and the "Menu" button should be located down further on the remote. The fast forward and skip buttons are perfectly positioned and the skip buttons have a notable bump on them to differentiate between the two.

The screen is actually better than I thought it would be. I can make out the display with or without my (fulltime) glasses. On the down side, it is very easy to tap on the wrong display icon when moving left and right through the screens. When this happens, depending on what you accidentally pressed, it takes a while to recover and get back to what you were watching. Some things may have turned on or off and if you weren't pointing in the right direction during the errant tap, good luck getting everything synced again.

Device Support:

The Harmony 900 claims thousands of supported devices. But good luck finding some of them. Instead of having a simple model number look up, you first have to choose the type of type of device, then the manufacturer followed by the model number. The problem is some devices are not listed in the device type or seem to be randomly added to device types you would not expect them in. There is an example in the set section below.

One thing clearly missing is a simple list of all the devices. In some cases like the X-10 IR interface module listed in many of these reviews, it is no longer available. It would be great to just enter X-10 and see every device that was compatible so you could buy the right one as an interface with the Harmony. There is no way to do this. This is a glaring omission that seems very simple to correct. Heck, a downloadable PDF would be better than nothing.

But all that said, I found every device in my house in their database and I had some fairly obscure AV stuff. And as long as the device is IR, you can custom map from any remote to the Harmony, so there really isn't any IR that cant work.

Setup:

Now I wasn't bragging when I said I was an IT professional. I simply mentioned this fact so those who are technically challenged have a baseline to consider when evaluating their ability to use and set up this device. I have built servers, computers, configured high end routers and switches and oversee hundreds of devices in several locations. And it always amazes me when I get a new piece of equipment like this, how frustrated I can get in the first few minutes of using it.

As others have mentioned, you have to install the software and set up an account to use the device. All settings are done interactively and in real time through the internet. If you don't have an internet connection, don't bother with this remote. I did not use the CD but instead downloaded the latest version from the Logitech web site. I also pre downloaded the owners manual several days before the remote arrived and read it cover to cover. So by the time I had it in my hand I was fairly comfortable with how the setup process should work. The software and driver installation was very easy and there were no USB connection problems to the remote. So far painless!

After letting the remote charge for a couple of hours I started through the setup process. I had used my own version of their worksheet and had all the devices written down. The first thing to note, again as other have mentioned is the Sony PS3 requires an add-on device to translate the IR to the Sony's native RF. Although Logitech sells such a device for almost 100.00, I already had a Nyko Media Hub for the PS3. It doesn't have all the functions of the Logitech, but it was only $17.00 and does all I need. And best of all, the Harmony 900 has the Nyko in it's database. The Roku2 XS is mysteriously placed in the DVD section and if I hadn't read some of these reviews I would not have known that. All the other devices mentioned above were in the database and all were added without an issue.

Once all the devices were added the software prompts you to add activities. Activities are the heart of the 900's functionality. However you must understand the concept of "Activities" and how they work to really get the most out of this remote. In a nutshell, an Activity is started by pressing a single button or in this case an icon like "Watch TV" . When you press Watch TV, the TV turns on and switches to the proper input, the Cable box turns on, the receiver turns on and switches to the proper input and output, and finally the 900 becomes a remote for all of those devices at the same time. More on this later.

To get a feel for this device I decided I would first set up all my devices without any activities. Essentially I wanted to just have a remote and be ability to go to one device after the other and see if they worked correctly. At first the software stumped me and didn't appear to let me get past setting up activities. I gave up trying and set some of them up thinking I could always wipe the remote clean and start again. I am not sure where I went wrong but the first activity I set up, "Watch TV" didn't work out so well. The TV didn't turn on, the Cable box turned off, etc. I ran back and forth from my PC to the living room about a dozen times and finally gave up for the night after about 2 hours of head banging. That night I re-read the manual, had the whole next day to ponder and went at it again .

The next morning I deleted all the activities and created them on my own, not using the wizard. I created an Activity, added the devices and then one by one told the software what I wanted each device to do. This was very helpful. I realized this not only got me the expected result, but it made me see how this software and remote really worked. After playing around for about 30 minutes I was able to create several of my most frequent activates. Going back to the equipment I pressed Watch TV. Again the TV did not turn on. If I used the Harmony for that device directly it worked. Back to the PC and set the activity to turn on the TV first. Still no luck. Next I tried the activity and used the on screen help. It asked if the TV turned on, I answered no and presto the TV turned on. After selects "this fixed my problem" on the remote, it worked every time. But; after each change on the PC I had to go through this help processes. I still do not know what the Harmony is doing to correct this.

Once I got all the basic Activities working I found a few other glitches. When I wanted to watch my combo DVF/VCR and use the VCR portion, none of the commands worked. It turns out this device has separate and distinct commands for FF-VCR and FF-DVD. The Harmony set all the DVD commands to that Activity by Default. I simply created two activities, One Watch VHS and one watch DVD even though it's the same source. In fact I found creating different activities for the same source is the answer to everyone complaining about missing the macro feature. It really does the same thing.

Now that I was on a roll my last bit of programming was renaming the activities. If you want the rest of your family to know how to use this thing without a PowerPoint presentation and tutor, I suggest you name the activities in such a way that its very obvious. Examples are Watch TV, Watch Netflix, Use PC, Listen to iPod, Listen to Pandora, etc. Since my receiver has an iPod dock, the Listen to iPod activity changed the source from whatever it is on to the receivers iPod port and then shows all the different music listening modes on the soft buttons. Watch Netflix switches to my Roku, etc.

Now for the best part of the Harmony setup! Its the ability to have the remote on the "Watch TV" activity and being able to program the hard and soft buttons to any other device's remote function. No more switching to the specific device's remote to change an often used setting on that device. If you take your time, you will eventually never have to use the "Devices" soft button as all the things you do will be setup in the Activity you are in. Now this takes some time and trial and error, but it's a huge time saver. Here is an example: You are Watching TV, controlling the sound options and volume with the Receiver, changing channels with the DVR and changing the aspect ration with the TV all on the same keypad. But beware! You can set what buttons do what on the device settings, but that won't change what they do in an Activity. The remote buttons MUST be set up in the Activity to work properly.

I spent several more days fine tuning the remote and now have not touched it in a while. I have a few more tweaks I am thinking of doing. And I would love to find the glitch that makes the TV turn on after I make any updates to the remote. Maybe a call is in order before my 90 days runs out.

USE:

As mentioned above, the ability to have the most common functions for several devices on one remote mode at the same time is huge! Now that I have used it for a couple of weeks, I have gotten accustomed to the button layout and can operate it without looking at it for most basic functions.

When everything is off and you select Watch TV, everything turns on and goes to the right inputs etc. However starting an activity can take quite a while. The remote can not be used while the Activity is being implemented. In my case I am already watching TV with sound on and the remote is still spinning the hour glass for a while. If you have the TV on too loud, you have to wait until the Harmony is done thinking or walk over and turn it down manually. However once that first activity is complete, any subsequent activity is changed fairly quick.

The battery life seems a bit short. I used to change the batteries in my remote once a year. This thing needs to be charged almost every day. If you let it go dead, its time to break out the old remotes during a recharge.

Once set up properly the Harmony 900 is very easy to use and the rest of the family had no problems with it, well almost.

Wife Problems:If your wife, child, etc. has a habit of turning the TV and other equipment on and off manually, you are in for some headaches. Since the Harmony remembers the last state of your devices (if you use it exclusively), it may turn things on instead of off, or off instead of on if someone else manually did that. My wife figured out the remote very quickly they way I have it set up. But she still does a mixture of using the remote and manual power buttons which frustrates both of us. Of course she blames the remote for not working properly when this happens. However anything that takes some blame from me is more than welcome.

RF Setup:

One of my misconceptions about this remote was the boasting of RF (Radio Frequency) capability. IT does indeed have IR capability. However, it does not have a database of RF codes like it does for IR codes. This device will not replace "ANY" RF remote, period. I was hoping there was a RF option for my X-10 home control devices, but that is not the case. For setups like this you need to get a IR to RF converted for the devices you already have. Figuring out which one you need can be a daunting task (See Device Support above).

The only RF device the Harmony will control directly is the IR blaster that comes with the device. An additional IR blaster can also be added. By default the IR blaster emits all the signals the remote puts out through IR to any and all blasters you have set up. You can control which blaster gets which signal. But this can only be done at the remote, not in the software. I am not sure why this is, but it is one of several deficiencies in the software.

Overall:

I went from wanting to return the Harmony 900 within hours of taking it out of the box, to protecting it like it is one of my children. I really love the Harmony 900 and would recommend it to most people. Those with little patients or difficulty working the microwave should avoid it unless someone else can set it up for you. It's overkill on a simply setup, like DVR and TV. But it is a pure joy if you have a medium to complex setup like I do. At $250.00 it is very pricy and hard to justify for a remote. But it seems to solve all my remote issues and to me it's worth it. I give it 4 stars.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Harmony 900 Rechargeable Remote with Color Touch Screen (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

GAOMON PD2200 130% sRGB Full-Laminated Pen Display with 8192 Battery-Free Tilt-Support Stylus 8 Touch Buttons -21.5'' Graphics Drawing Tablet Monitor with Adjustable Stand I am a huge supporter of open source graphics software because I feel that the leading brand name software uses their virtual monopoly to bully people into overpriced, restrictive, nonsensical subscription programs. When I saw that this tablet was listed as being compatible with GIMP and most other graphics programs, I felt comfortable purchasing it for my uses.

However, upon installing it, I found that it is not actually compatible with the vast majority of graphic software except for those supported by Adobe, and a couple of other inferior programs. To clarify, it will still "function" with most programs, but only as a basic mouse. It will not support pressure sensitivity nor tilt. This, in my mind, means that it is NOT compatible, as pressure and tilt are essential functions for any illustrator. Without them, this is basically just a glorified mouse pad.

From Gaomon's troubleshooting website regarding lack of pressure sensitivity:

"The version of your drawing program might be too low to support pen pressure. Please upload it or try to draw in other drawing programs. Here do we suggest you some drawing programs. For windows system: Adobe Photoshop CC, Adobe Photoshop CC 2015, Adobe Photoshop CC 2017, Adobe Photoshop CC 2018, Adobe Photoshop cs5，Adobe Photoshop cs6, Adobe Animate CC2017 For Mac system: Adobe Photoshop CC, Adobe Photoshop CC 2015, Adobe Photoshop CC 2017, Adobe Photoshop cs5, Adobe Photoshop cs6, Adobe illustrator cs6, Adobe Flash Professional CC, Adobe Animate CC 2018 Other free drawing programs: Sai, Krita, FireAlpaca"

Contrast that with the information in the product listing, which says, "compatible with most of major drawing software such as Photoshop、SAI version 2、Illustrator、krita、firealpaca、gimp、SketchBook Pro、MediBang Paint Pro, etc."

GIMP and others are clearly listed, but are not actually compatible. This is highly misleading.

As for other aspects of the tablet, I can't say too much as I haven't used it very much due to this issue. However, from what I have found so far, the display looks good, and the set up is pretty straightforward, although their manual is extremely confusing to try to follow.

The buttons on the side of the display are completely smooth and can not be felt; there is nothing there to help you locate them by tactile means, so you will have to stop looking at your work and visually find them in order to use them. They are also located such that they are easily pressed accidentally when adjusting the position of your tablet, which gets annoying pretty quickly.

The chords that come with the tablet are a bit short, maybe 4 or 5 feet, which doesn't allow for much room to position your tablet if you use a PC that is located beneath your desk or to the side, especially if the hook-up ports are on the back of the PC. You can of course buy replacement chords.

The stylus is very lightweight, which I personally consider a positive but some people may prefer a heftier stylus.

There is not much lag when using the stylus; the movement is smooth enough for my needs. The pressure sensitivity, when tested in a diagnostic program, seems quite good as well. It just doesn't work with the software I hoped to use it with.

Overall the tablet is a nice size and has a nice display, but the other issues are factors you should consider when deciding between this tablet and a more expensive brand.
text_fidelity_b: GAOMON PD2200 130% sRGB Full-Laminated Pen Display with 8192 Battery-Free Tilt-Support Stylus 8 Touch Buttons -21.5'' Graphics Drawing Tablet Monitor with Adjustable Stand

CORSAIR Hydro Series H105 AIO Liquid CPU Cooler, 240mm Thick Radiator, Dual 120mm PWM Fans I've wanted to try one of these liquid CPU coolers for ages, but it always been a little too cheap to spend the extra money on one, and I confess I've been mildly concerned about using a liquid anything inside my computer. I'm glad I tried this out.

This particular model has a radiator style grate which the fan sits on (there is some conductive paste included), then has tubes leading to the cooler unit. The water is totally enclosed in the system, and I can see no danger of leakage. The fan is quiet and unobtrusive.

It has a four pin connector, so if your computer has a four pin connector as well, your computer can control the speed of the fan. However, the four pin connector can also connect to a three pin connector and it works fine, you just lose that extra bit of control.

The one small improvement I'd like to see is that the water/cooling area only goes to one side of the radiator type grate, not around all of the edges, so one side of it will always be hotter than the other. It still disperses heat well, just seems like a less efficient system then it could be.

Lastly, I love the thumbscrews included for installing. I hate dealing with normal screws, and the thumbscrews are such a thoughtful touch that it made me think well of the company for including them.

Overall, if you've been on the fence about testing out one of these new liquid CPU coolers, I don't see any reason not to try out this one. The price is reasonable for what it is, and it looks like a highly effective setup, certainly better than just using a fan.
text_fidelity_b: CORSAIR Hydro Series H105 AIO Liquid CPU Cooler, 240mm Thick Radiator, Dual 120mm PWM Fans

text_fidelity_a:
Luby Portable Movie Projector with Free Projector Screen Perfect for Fun Camping Neighborhood Gathering Backyard Movie The listing says this projector supports 1920 X 1080p resolution. It doesn't say it projects in that resolution. And it doesn't. You can see the pixel grid on the home screen. It's definitely not a 1080p projector. I don't even think it's 720p. Text is pretty blurry when you connect it to a computer as a monitor. If you do that, you might want to enlarge the font for readability.

Brightness is pretty good. It's better than mini projectors I've seen in the past. But the room (or outdoors, if you're using it there) will need to be pretty dark to get a good view. The farther away the projector is from the screen, the bigger the picture, the more spread out the light is, the darker the room will need to be to see it.

I had hopes the OS would play DVDs directly from a USB-powered outboard DVD player, but it doesn't have that functionality. I tried it and it would not recognize the connected device. You do have to manually select the input from the home screen. There are multiple inputs: HDMI, VGA, micro SD card, and USB.

The included screen is okay, but a white wall (or even ceiling) works well too.

On the bottom of the projector is a tripod mounting hole, a nice addition.

The manual keystone adjustment works only for up and down adjustment, not side to side. The focus is also manual, and works well.

The two negatives to me are that the remote control pretty much has to be aimed directly at the IR receiver ports on the projector to get it to work (there are ports on the front and back), and there is some trash inside the lens that shows up in the projected image in the one I received. I'll have to open up the projector to blow that out.

Other than that, at this price point, it's a good projector, and pretty versatile in terms of portability and input options.
text_fidelity_b: Luby Portable Movie Projector with Free Projector Screen Perfect for Fun Camping Neighborhood Gathering Backyard Movie

The sound quality is good, I’ve been using them with music and streaming shows, and I haven’t been disappointed with the sound quality.

I’m not as pleased with the short battery life, touch controls, and lack of audio cues.

I get about 2-3 hours of playback per charge. It’s rare for me to battery drain earbuds, but with this pair, I hear the low battery chime every time I use them.

The touch controls and lack of audio cues go together. The touch controls are super easy to activate on accident. More than once I’ve taken the earbuds out only to find I hit Play while doing so, and they kept playing music. I also activate random controls when adjusting the earbuds in my ears … and I don’t always know what I’ve done. Did I turn ANC on or off? The audio cues are just beeps, not an announcement like “ANC on/ANC off.”

I like the design of the case. It has a sliding top, so you can actually clean the entire area where the earbuds sit. When you put the earbuds inside the case, a light flashes to show their battery level. The case charges wirelessly or via USB-C. There’s only one LED light on the outside of the case, it’s easy to miss when you’re trying to see if the case is charging or not.

While I have been partial to KEF in the past for speakers, the performance of this Polk has really wow'd me. At present I'm using this center speaker with KEF left and right front speakers, and KEF for surround. I've been so impressed with the ES35 that I'll be changing to Polk for my L/R soon, and keep the KEF only for surround (5.1.2 setup).

An excellent center speaker that hits the mark on all counts. Five stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) I received a Kindle as a gift, and it has taken over my reading life. I'm sad when a book is only available in print and delighted when there is a Kindle version. It's not AS comfortable as a print book, it's MORE comfortable than a print book. The font is amazing. It's easy to use, and for people who knit, it sits nicely in a bookstand on or a reader's pillow to read while knitting.

I have the Sony eReader. I used to own the rocket. I see the Kindle as the real future of ebooks, and I really want ebooks to succeed for a few reasons.

One is storage. If you are a bibliophile, you probably have a book army ready to take over your home. We avid readers are forced to cull our libraries to make room for new books. No more. I would suggest opening a free account with a service like Goodreads to categorize books, since with the Kindle you can't set up a "history" section and a "fantasy" section, but that's so minor. I never could keep those organized in my print library as well, and many books fall into multiple categories anyway. Do I need to mention that ebooks don't yellow and decay over time?

Two is portability. If you are the type to carry many books at once (I am--some for study and some for pleasure reading along with a newspaper) then this is the easiest way to do it.

Three is the glorious possibility that books will never go "out of print" again, because there is no "print" overhead, just a little meg sitting in a several terrabyte raid array somewhere. Books will always be a minute away.

Four is the idea that books will be instantly large print and still small, and easy to tote around. My eyes are still quite good, but I'd love to think, when age degrades them someday, I'll still be able to read the latest releases easily.

Five is the instant availability of hot books. When Brisingr came out, it was sitting on my Kindle that morning. Compare that to the sometimes day-long wait we went through for the Harry Potter books (and books that size are yet another reason ebooks rock). I love having the New York Times delivered, but can't stand it when the delivery boy loses the key and rings my bell at 4 in the morning. This is the best of both worlds.

Six is the ease of reading large online documents, such as those from Gutenberg or a friend's novel (and don't we all have someone who sends us large files to read from time to time?)

Seven is the price of the books. Everything is cheaper on the Kindle and some books are frighteningly inexpensive. I bought the Talmud for 99 cents. A collection of the first five books in the John Carter on Mars series for 99 cents. And the entire collection of the Wizard of Oz books for, you guessed it, 99 cents.

Other e-readers hit close to the mark; the Kindle got it right. I only want two things. I want color and I want Amazon to hit that goal of having every book (including comics and manga please) available for the Kindle. Overall, the day of the ebook truly arrived with the Kindle and I couldn't be happier.
text_fidelity_b: Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)

text_fidelity_a:
KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black Overall this keyboard is great. The keys feel nice and they're quiet but not too quiet or soft or squishy. Enjoy typing on this keyboard, pushing the keys seems to take minimal effort and overall it's great.

The best part about the keyboard is that it separates and having the ability to give it a little separation is great. I miss it when I don't have it and it helps avoid torquing the wrists when you are typing. I also love the feel of the keys.

Now before my minor complaints understand two things: (1) I really like this keyboard and despite what I would consider minor defects, I would definitely buy another one. (2) please excuse the fact that I like my keyboards to be consistent and while Apple may not make the *best* keyboards I do use a laptop and I am used to their keyboard layout and feel.

The biggest thing that annoyed me when I purchased this keyboard was the positioning of the ⌘ (command) key. It seems to be shifted over a bit from what I'm used to. Normally I would hit ⌘ with my thumb but it's a little touch to do that on this one given the position of it. It's just something I'm having to get used to.

One minor downside to the keyboard is that the function key doesn't work the same way as the default apple keyboard, rather, the `fn` key is a toggle. I prefer for fn to work as a modifier because that is what I am used to on my laptop keyboard.

Another minor problem is the styling on the caps lock key. Like many people, I remap my caps lock to ctrl and and thus want caps lock to be a normal button. However, on this keyboard the caps lock key is missing the right part of the key so that you don't accidentally hit it when typing the `a` key.

Finally, the escape key and '`' (back tick) keys are in weird positions. The escape key is not as bad as the backtick. There is just something about the distance that I must go that is different from what I'm used to and I have been consistently hitting the `1` key instead. Life goes on.
text_fidelity_b: KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black

Razer Opus Active Noise Cancelling ANC Wireless Headphones: THX Audio Tuning - 25 Hr Battery - Bluetooth 4.2 & 3.5mm Jack Compatible - Auto Play/Auto Pause - Carrying Case Included - Midnight Blue At first glance, the Razer Opus ANC Wireless Headphones don’t look like a Razer product. Where’s the green? Where’s the RGB? Even the branding is subdued.

These headphones are a grown-up Razer product, probably meant to be headphones you can take anywhere and not stick out as a gamer.

The Midnight Blue color is a nice change from black. I have a few pairs of wireless headphones and every single pair is black, so I appreciate having a little variety. Midnight Blue is a very deep blue -- so deep it’s almost black.

I’ve been trying the Opus headphones out for a few weeks and they have become the headphones I use every day. Before, I was using the Sony XB900N.

My favorite thing about the Opus headphones is how comfortable they are. The headband and ear cups have cushy padding. The headphones don’t squeeze my head too tight and don’t weigh a lot. I can wear these for 5+ hours at a time and not get a headache.

Sound quality is decent. I mostly use the Opus for listening to music and TV/movies. Compared to Razer’s gaming headsets, this isn’t one I’d pick for serious gaming. There is a tiny bit of lag and the low, deep sounds aren’t as punchy as with say, a Razer Kraken headset.

Razer’s claim of up to 25 hours of battery life seems pretty accurate. I didn’t keep a log every time I used the headphones, but I was able to use them for 4-5 hours a day for a good week before needing to charge. Unfortunately there is no battery indicator on the headphones to know when the battery is running low.

I don’t love the Razer Opus app needed to tweak a few of the settings. I have an older Android phone running Nougat, the app is incompatible with my phone. So I had to borrow my mom’s iPhone to install the app. By default, the headphones shut off after 5 minutes and I could only change this setting in the app. The app also allows you to switch between a few audio presets (but you can’t create your own) and check battery life.

If I take the headphones off my head, they automatically pause whatever I’m watching or listening to. I like this; my mom often talks to me when I’m wearing headphones, so it’s a lot quicker to just take them off and now I don’t have to manually pause. This is a setting that can be changed in the app.

The Active Noise Cancelling is what I expect for a pair of headphones in this price range. It’s decent. Not great, not horrible, but good enough to mute most background noise. But I don’t like that there’s not a light or indicator on the headphones to tell when I have ANC turned on.

The Opus doesn’t support Bluetooth multipoint.

The headphones charge via USB-C. The included case stores the headphones, charging cable, USB-C to USB A adapter, 3.5 mm audio cable, and airline adapter. The case actually has an outline on the bottom to tell you how to fit the headphones inside.
text_fidelity_b: Razer Opus Active Noise Cancelling ANC Wireless Headphones: THX Audio Tuning - 25 Hr Battery - Bluetooth 4.2 & 3.5mm Jack Compatible - Auto Play/Auto Pause - Carrying Case Included - Midnight Blue

turelar Compatible Headphone Jack Dongle Adapter for Phone X 8/8plus 7/7plus I'm really impressed with this bluetooth receiver. Unlike another brand I tried, this offers outstanding sound quality, which is my main reason for using it.

It's very straightforward to set up. Just plug in the receiver (it's very small - less bulky than most "wall warts" that are present on power plugs), pair it with your bluetooth source, and plug the included cables into a stereo.

I'm using this with a Kindle Fire 8.9. Pairing was quick and simple.

The connection to the stereo can be done via a single cable or using a two cable (L/R) setup. Cables for both options are included. I'm using the L/R option, and plugged the cables into the TAPE input on my stereo receiver.

The sound quality is excellent. It is very hard to tell the difference in quality when streaming audio via this receiver versus playing a CD on the receiver. Movie dialog was outstanding as well.

The fact that it does not require a battery is a plus and a minus. On the plus side, no need to worry about recharging or swapping batteries. On the down side, it was a bit of a problem for me to get the cables routed since the wall outlet near my stereo is not easily accessible. I wound up running a short extension cord so that I could plug in the receiver close enough to the stereo so that the L/R cables would reach.

As a bonus, it includes a USB port so you can use it to recharge your phone/tablet/etc.

That one minor issue aside, I'm very impressed with the performance of this product. Highly recommend.

text_fidelity_a:
Philips BT2500B/37 Wireless Portable Speaker I have owned those annoying bluetooth ear pieces that always feel like they're about to fall off - or actually do. And although the sound varies from product to product, it's just not a system I am comfortable with.

This little speaker is simply perfect for my needs. It is 4 inches by 4 inches wide and only 1 inch thick. It has a switch that you slide to the right when you wish to enable the bluetooth, or to the left to turn it off. There is also another small button right beside the switch that you push in to receive or disconnect a call. A silver volume knob is sleekly incorporated in the overal design. The pairing was instant and consistant. No need to type in some code or wait forever for them to find each other. But here's the most important part - I hear my calls clearly and with no drop off or fade.

In all fairness, I only use this in my car and I don't spend ridiculous amounts of time on my phone when I'm driving. I've used other products with useless results. Half of the time I would risk a ticket by just ditching the ear piece and talking on my cell. In this case, I'm able to place it on the seat next to me and converse without any problems. Now that it's passed my tests, I'll be getting some velcro and mounting it to my dash board when I'm driving, and then just popping it in the glove compartment when I'm done.

The unit comes with a USB charger cable and it had a partial charge when I received it. Once it's fully charged and you turn it on, a blue light will blink for about 2 seconds and then go to a solid blue. According to the enclosed instructions, you will know that the battery is low when it blinks red. Couldn't be easier.

Musically speaking, my JBL and Sony are better designed for that purpose. But as a compact, speaker phone - this Phillips is without equal. Hands-free clarity without an annoying piece of plastic hanging over your ear. What more could you ask?
text_fidelity_b: Philips BT2500B/37 Wireless Portable Speaker

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Harmony Smart Control with Smartphone App and Simple All in One Remote - Black Build and Setup:
This is a very solid remote. Well constructed. It takes a disk watch type battery that is activated when you remove the tab. The lines are clean and elegant, and it feels well constructed.

Set up was very simple. I simply logged into myharmony.com and choose the Add a remote option.

The difference between this remote and other Harmony remotes is that this has a hub and blaster units that connects through your wireless network to allow you to connect and control your units with your smartphone.

You have to connect the hub and blaster unit around the units you want to control. It has to be connected to your home wireless network, which was easy. You can either do it through myharmony.com or by pressing the setup button on the hub and your router (if it supports it) it was that easy.

This particular unit controls my TV, Dish DVR, and VCR/DVD combo. Setting it up for the units was quite easy.

Using the Remote:
One selling point this has over the Ultimate is that the number buttons are solid state buttons, unlike the touch screen buttons on the Ultimate. As much as I like the touch screen technology, having buttons you can press by touch is a plus for.

There are also traditional DVR buttons, fast forward, as well as red, blue yellow, and green buttons. Since this remote did not have a 30 second advance button, and I rely on that, I programmed a short press of the green and yellow buttons to act as the skip forward. I programmed long pressing those buttons to do the default actions of those buttons. I appreciated that you could customize in that way.

Phone App:
The phone app for the android is a bit lacking as it is not quite as sophisticated as the remote itself, but can do most of the actions of the remote as long as you are connected to the same wireless network as your hub is.

Troubleshooting:
The remote is easy to use and troubleshoot, Simply rebooting or re-syncing the remote can resolve most problems I've found. It also prompts you for assistance the first time you add an action or new device.

Overall this is a great remote. This will demand, though, some knowledge on your part as it is a very sophisticated remote. Many problems that occur can easily be resolved by some knowledge of networks, remotes, or Harmony devices in general. If you have experience with this you will enjoy the functions and capacity of this remote.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Harmony Smart Control with Smartphone App and Simple All in One Remote - Black
